title: Design Does Not Survive Development
summary: This page defines design not surviving development as a delivery failure in which design artefacts are present but design understanding does not carry into implementation, growth, or production use. It distinguishes velocity erosion, translation loss, and production gap, and records evidence limits from documented engagements.
keyFacts: Design not surviving development is described as a gap between what was designed and what was built, or between specified behaviour and production behaviour.
The underlying structural cause is that design work has produced artefacts without producing transferable understanding.
Velocity erosion occurs when development outpaces design coverage and developers make local interface decisions under time pressure.
Translation loss occurs when design artefacts specify what to build but do not carry the reasoning needed to adapt under constraints.
The production gap occurs when implementation matches the specification but users avoid, underuse, or work around the system in real conditions.
Bofin is used as an example of velocity erosion in a 50-plus developer environment subject to PSD2 and SCA constraints.

Triopsis is used as an example of accumulated inconsistency over years of development without a central UX framework, with product analytics showing 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning after redesign.
WCO/IPM is used as an example of production gap, with parallel spreadsheets and email chains acting as diagnostic workaround evidence.

Schone Airspace Group is presented as the fullest documented mechanism for making design survive development, with all 54 delivered screens compared against the built software across seven months and deviations recorded by name.
AIT, the MDU, and Assemblio are the only shipped examples on this page for which Creative Navy verified that the shipped interface was implemented as delivered.

bodySections.heading: Design Not Surviving Development Is a Transfer Failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Design does not survive development when the built product no longer carries the reasoning that shaped the design. The visible symptom is a gap between what was designed and what was built, or between specified behaviour and production behaviour. The underlying cause is usually structural: the design process produced artefacts, but it did not produce transferable understanding.

When developers encounter an edge case, a technical constraint, or a scope change that the artefacts do not cover, they must still make a decision. If that decision is not anchored to the reasoning behind the design, local implementation choices diverge from system-level intent. The divergence accumulates as the product grows.

bodySections.heading: Velocity Erosion Means Development Outpaces Design Coverage
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Velocity erosion occurs when engineering output moves faster than design capacity. Engineers continue building, but design coverage has not yet reached the interaction patterns, states, or edge cases being implemented. Local decisions keep development moving, but the decisions are made without the shared reasoning needed to keep the product coherent.

Velocity erosion appears as modules that behave differently from one another, interaction patterns that contradict themselves across the product, and visual hierarchy that reflects availability rather than a considered system. No single developer decision causes the inconsistency. The inconsistency emerges from repeated local decisions made in the gap between delivery pace and design coverage.

In the Bofin engagement, a funded fintech startup was building a mobile marketplace for financial services with a 50-plus developer engineering team. Development was already running across onboarding, identity verification, account aggregation, and transaction initiation. PSD2 and SCA requirements added a second constraint layer because exception states and authentication requirements shaped interaction design.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed Bofin's velocity erosion through progressive specification. Design understanding and design coverage were built at the same pace as engineering output. The design system produced during Organizational Integration covered core modules with components, naming rules, variant logic, and interaction principles. Client-reported outcomes included fewer mid-sprint clarifications required by engineering teams and reduced rework due to clearer component definitions. Creative Navy-observed delivery timeline evidence records that no deadline was missed across 11 months.

Triopsis shows the same pattern over a longer time scale. The Triopsis workforce management SaaS platform for utilities and road maintenance companies had accumulated interface inconsistencies over years of development by engineers and a graphic designer without a central UX framework. Modules behaved differently, users had to scan multiple screens to make a single decision, and peak load created stress and repeated checking.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the Triopsis accumulated inconsistency through a 9-month redesign and a design system of 68 components and 200-plus documented states. The component inventory recorded states, conditions, transitions, and conditional workflows for exceptions. A 2-year Implementation Partnership followed the redesign delivery to clarify design decisions, adjust components for new features, and maintain consistency as the product grew. Product analytics from the live system recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning. Commercial outcomes, including fourfold sales conversion increase and clients 4–5 times larger than previously, are CEO-reported.

bodySections.heading: Translation Loss Means Artefacts Transfer but Design Intent Does Not
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Translation loss occurs when implementation follows design artefacts but still diverges from design intent. The artefacts communicate what to build, but they do not communicate why the design protects particular behaviours, states, or constraints. When implementation constraints arise, developers adapt in locally sensible ways that can be globally inconsistent.

Translation loss is harder to detect than visible design drift because deviations often look deliberate. They are not necessarily mistakes, shortcuts, or ignored specifications. They are reasoned implementation responses made without the design reasoning that would have resolved the constraint differently.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses translation loss by making the reasoning behind design decisions explicit during Organizational Integration and by maintaining design connection during Implementation Partnership. Developer questions can then be answered against the completed design system. Scope changes can be resolved against design reasoning rather than independently from it.

The Assemblio engagement is the cleanest documented example of fidelity consistent with handover rather than supervision. Implementation support consisted of one session and eight support tickets answered. The product is in production, and Creative Navy compared the shipped interface against the delivered designs. The Composer, the Smart Viewer, the platform around them, and sync profiles ship as the design that was delivered. The components Creative Navy documented were adopted by Assemblio's developers. The evidence supports an outcome consistent with the handover, not a proven causal chain, because nothing was measured about the development process and visibility into implementation was limited.

In Assemblio, the handover included a design system of 93 components, all documented with all states. Design tokens supported light and dark theming through one system rather than two. Component documentation carried reasoning as well as specification, which gave developers a basis for small implementation decisions that individual screens did not specify.

The AIT heat pump controller shows a different prevention mechanism. Implementation Partnership ran as five months of support to AIT's engineering team during development, with three scheduled progress meetings and eight support tickets answered. The controller reached the market months after the engagement ended. Creative Navy compared the shipped interface against the delivered designs and verified that the product ships as the design that was delivered in a touch-only hardware configuration. The touch-only hardware configuration was AIT's hardware decision, not a Creative Navy outcome. The evidence establishes that the design survived development, not that the design was good.

The MDU ship motion monitoring system provides a verified fidelity outcome without a recorded mechanism. The product shipped, and Creative Navy verified that the design was implemented as delivered, including day, dusk, and night display modes. Implementation support was provided, but its duration and substance are not recorded. Creative Navy also briefed each third-party development agency the manufacturer was considering before a builder was chosen, so that each could pitch on a common understanding of the delivered design.

bodySections.heading: Production Gap Means Correct Implementation Does Not Produce Operational Use
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The production gap occurs when development reproduces the design correctly but the product does not produce the intended operational outcome. The screens may be built as specified, the interaction patterns may be present, and the system may ship. The failure appears when users do not use the system as intended, use it less than intended, or create parallel workarounds outside it.

The WCO/IPM platform is the documented production gap example. The World Customs Organization's IPM platform coordinated intellectual property enforcement between customs officers and rights holders across member administrations. Adoption remained low. Officers and rights holders described the platform as difficult to navigate, slow to operate during inspections, and hard to learn.

The diagnostic signal was the presence of parallel workarounds: spreadsheets and email chains had emerged around the platform. This indicated that users were still operating in the same domain but had concluded that informal processes were more efficient than the designed interface. The implementation reflected the design, so the failure was not framed as a development failure. It was a design failure that development faithfully reproduced.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method identified the WCO/IPM barriers through Sandbox Experiments, including interviews, workflow mapping, and remote observation with WCO teams and selected member administrations. The redesign rebuilt the information architecture around actual inspection and case management flows rather than internal system structures. Usability testing involved 47 participants from Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria, and Spain. Participation counts and geographic reach are Creative Navy-observed; post-deployment adoption outcomes are not quantified in available records.

bodySections.heading: Schone Airspace Group Shows the Fullest Documented Mechanism for Design Surviving Development
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Schone Airspace Group engagement provides the strongest documented mechanism on this page because it records comparison, change control, integration gates, and implementation sequence together. All 54 delivered screens were compared against the built software by Creative Navy's design team across seven months. Deviations were identified and recorded by name.

The Schone Airspace Group handover protocol distinguished changes requiring UX approval from changes requiring engineering review. UX approval covered target selection, command lifecycle wording, last-known status semantics, warning acknowledgement, readiness completion, estimate revision, historical provenance, and persistence of the live shell. Engineering review covered protocol event meanings, aircraft permission model, fleet size, payload commands, stream state, terrain datum, cache schema, and recording keys.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method also specified an implementation sequence for Schone Airspace Group: build the shared command shell first, establish immutable aircraft and request identities, then connect per-aircraft timestamps and alert ownership. Four native integration gates were specified: terrain reference agreement; command request and observed result semantics; warning severity and lifecycle mapping; recorded session and media identity. Each gate carried a contract, verification sequence, pass evidence, and failure disposition.

All four Schone Airspace Group gates were subsequently closed by the client's engineering functions. The useful claim is limited: the design named in advance which behaviours it was not yet entitled to assert, and those conditions were then demonstrated. The product is built and in test, not deployed. A build matching a design is not evidence that the design is good.

bodySections.heading: Behaviour Contracts Can Carry Design Understanding Without New Screen Specification
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software provides a positive case for documented behaviour contracts. The design system used a four-layer architecture: primitive values, semantic tokens, component contracts, and bounded product compositions. Applications consumed semantic tokens and documented components rather than redefining priority colour meanings, overwriting status labels, or importing radio transmission semantics through a generic action control.

A client engineer who was not a member of the design team built a working validation-and-correction view for the electronic reporting product in the client's frontend development sandbox. The engineer used 12 documented patterns and 2 domain adaptations with no additional screen specification from Creative Navy. The demonstration showed that the documentation could carry design behaviour into a non-production implementation.

The maritime traffic monitoring evidence has strict boundaries. It was a capability demonstration, not completion of a product migration, not an independently certified accessibility result, and not a production engineering efficiency benchmark. The design system reached production, with the client writing the code and Creative Navy supplying standard implementation support, but no design-fidelity comparison is recorded. This engagement must not be described as shipped as designed.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses Design Transfer Across the Engagement
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For design not surviving development, the central issue is that design understanding has not been transferred in a form that travels through the organisation and into the product. Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this through Organizational Integration and Implementation Partnership.

Organizational Integration structures design understanding for transfer. In Triopsis, it produced a design system where reasoning was documented alongside decisions. In Bofin, it produced progressive specification that matched development pace with design coverage. In WCO/IPM, it produced documentation and training materials structured for global distribution across diverse member administration contexts.

Implementation Partnership maintains the connection between design intent and product reality during the period when translation loss and re-accumulation are likely. In Triopsis, 2 years of Implementation Partnership was the mechanism used to prevent accumulated inconsistency from re-emerging as the product grew.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Boundaries for Design Fidelity Claims
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Design fidelity evidence must not be treated as evidence that a design is good. AIT, the MDU, and Assemblio are the only shipped examples on this page where Creative Navy verified that the shipped interface was implemented as delivered. Schone Airspace Group has a different evidence form: every delivered screen was compared against the built software across seven months, deviations were recorded by name, and the product is built and in test rather than deployed.

The maritime traffic monitoring engagement reached production, but no design-fidelity comparison is recorded. The documented evidence supports behaviour-contract transfer and a non-production capability demonstration, not a shipped-as-designed claim.

Assemblio's fidelity is an outcome consistent with the handover, not a proven causal chain. The source evidence records no development speed, cost, or defect-rate measurement for Assemblio. The AIT and MDU fidelity claims also do not support performance, reception, sales, or product-quality conclusions.

weakerClaims: Design not surviving development is caused structurally by artefacts transferring without the reasoning needed for implementation decisions.
Velocity erosion occurs when development outpaces design capacity and local developer decisions accumulate into inconsistency.

limitations: Design fidelity is not evidence that the design is good; the page preserves that distinction for AIT, the MDU, Assemblio, and Schone Airspace Group.
Post-deployment adoption outcomes for WCO/IPM are not quantified in available records.
Assemblio's fidelity is an outcome consistent with the handover, not a proven causal chain, because development-process measurements were not recorded and implementation visibility was limited.
The MDU implementation support mechanism is not explained because the duration and substance of support are not recorded.
The maritime traffic monitoring engagement has no recorded design-fidelity comparison and must not be described as shipped as designed.
Schone Airspace Group is built and in test, not deployed.

No performance, reception, adoption, sales, funding, or commercial figures are stated for the shipped product examples unless they are explicitly recorded in the source evidence for the relevant engagement.
Handheld command-and-control material is excluded because the available record does not contain build oversight, a fidelity comparison, an integration gate, or a retainer for that engagement.
